title: Hydrophobic Copper Interfaces Boost Electroreduction of Carbon Dioxide to Ethylene in Water
abstract: Cu is in the spotlight as it represents the only metal capable of catalyzing CO2 reduction to multicarbon products. However, its catalytic performance is determined collectively by a number of parameters including its composition and structure, electrolyte, and cell configuration. It remains a challenge to disentangle and understand the individual effect of these parameters. In this work, we study the effect of the electrode−electrolyte interface on CO2 reduction in water by coating CuO electrodes with polymers of varying hydrophilicities/ phobicities. Hydrophilic polymers such as poly(vinyl alcohol) and poly(vinylpyrrolidone) exert negligible influence, while hydrophobic polymers such as poly(vinylidene fluoride) and polyethylene significantly enhance the activity, selectivity, and stability of CuO-derived electrodes toward C2H4 production. From ex situ characterizations, electrolysis in deuterated water, and molecular dynamics simulations, we propose that the improved catalytic performance triggered by hydrophobic polymers originates from restricted water diffusion and a higher local pH near the electrode surface. These observations shed light on interfacial manipulation for promoted CO2-to-C2H4 conversion.

sections.text: KEYWORDS: CO2 reduction, interfacial hydrophobicity, polymer coating, water diffusion, ethylene production

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to value-added products offers a promising strategy to close the anthropogenic carbon cycle and store renewable energy.1,2
Over decades of efforts, CO and HCOOH can now be produced with high selectivity (>95%) from CO2RR on many metal-based catalysts (i.e., Au and Ag for CO, Bi and Sn for HCOOH).3−5 However, a significant challenge remains to selectively convert CO2 to ethylene,
6 a widely used chemical feedstock in the polymer industry, especially in the synthesis of polyethylene (PE).7 Furthermore, the only catalyst that can catalyze such conversion is Cu,8 although the selectivity toward C2H4 production is low to moderate. This lies in two aspects, i.e., (1) the competing water reduction to produce H2 and (2) the multiple reaction pathways to form a variety of C1−3 products such as CO, HCOOH, CH3OH, CH4, CH3COOH, C2H5OH, and C3H7OH. The former constitutes the major issue and leads to a selectivity loss of >30%,9,10 as water reduction to H2 takes place more readily than CO2RR.
11 In addition, water is in large excess, considering that [CO2] = 0.033 M and [H2O] = 55.6 M. 12
To optimize the CO2-to-C2H4 conversion in water, considerable efforts have been put into modifying the Cu composition and structure (i.e., oxide,13 alloy,14 size,15 shape,16 and crystallinity17), adjusting electrolyte (cation18 and anion19), and designing the electrochemical setup (gas diffusion electrode and flow cell).20 Recently, it has been recognized that the local environment of the electrode− electrolyte interface also plays a critical role in CO2RR. 21−25 In
the few reports with a focus on the electrode−electrolyte interface effect, organic molecules and polymers have been used to modify the Cu surface. For example, Xie et al. and Ahn et al. in their respective work found that the modification of Cu with amino acid26 and poly(acrylamide)27 could double the selectivity of CO2RR toward C2H4 production. The enhanced selectivity was ascribed to the stabilization of specific CO2RR intermediates (*CHO or *OC−CO) on the Cu surface through hydrogen bonding with the organic modifiers. In another work, Thevenon et al. reported that the formation of a N,N′-ethylene-phenanthrolinium-based organic layer on Cu improved the C2H4 selectivity by 3−4 times. Here, the organic layer played multiple functions by inducing the generation of cubelike copper nanostructures to facilitate C−C coupling.28 In such systems, the complex interplay among the abovementioned properties and conditions collectively determines the overall product selectivity on the Cu electrodes. Yet, the specific effect of the individual parameter is far from being fully understood. Any molecular systems coated on an electrode will influence
the interfacial chemistry at the surface, regardless of the chemical structure. Quantum mechanics calculations predict

31 Unfortunately, the selectivity increase came at the cost of a dramatic activity loss because of the surface modification. It should be mentioned that the formation of Cu−S bonding on the Cu surface also affects its electronic structure, which may bring other effects than hydrophobicity change into play. In this work, we investigate the influence of the electrode− electrolyte interface on CO2RR in water at an electrode constructed from CuO nanoparticles (NPs). This CuOderived electrode is modified with hydrophobic polymers such as poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF) and PE using a straightforward physical deposition protocol. Importantly, these inert polymers are unable to interact specifically with either the NPs or the CO2RR intermediates, thus excluding many other effects from coming into play and limiting the parameter space of potential contributors to the interface change. We demonstrate that the introduction of the hydrophobic polymer leads to a dramatic enhancement of not only the selectivity but also the activity and stability of the CO2-to-C2H4 conversion. Such performance enhancement is related to neither the change of morphology, crystallinity, or oxidation state of Cu nor the specific structure of the polymer. Instead, it is dictated by the hydrophobic environment created by the polymers that restrict water transport in the vicinity of the Cu surface. The disclosure in this work of the strong correlation between hydrophobicity, mass transport, and CO2RR selectivity is expected to open new avenues in the design of high-performance electrocatalysts for the CO2-toC2H4 conversion.

sections.heading: 2. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
The CuO−PVDF electrode was fabricated using PVDF (loading = 0.25 mg cm−2) to cover the CuO NPs deposited onto carbon support. Cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) indicates that the thickness of the CuO layer is ∼2 μm with a porous PVDF layer on top (Figure 1a). The latter layer consists of aggregated spherulite PVDF NPs with a diameter of 0.77 ± 0.14 μm (Figures 1b and S1). The coating of PVDF on CuO is further confirmed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and powder X-ray diffraction (XRD). In XPS, the strong F 1s peak at 688 eV and the two C 1s peaks at 290.9 and 286.4 eV are characteristic of fluorinated hydrocarbons (Figure 1c).32 Two other small C 1s peaks originate from adventitious carbons that are usually observed in XPS measurements.33 In XRD, two diffraction peaks at 36.3 and 43.2° pertain to PVDF (α-phase, JCPDS #42-1650, Figure 1d). Notably, the PVDF coating attenuates the diffraction peaks of monoclinic CuO at 35.5 and 38.6° significantly, as compared with the bare CuO electrode. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) shows that the CuO NPs feature a short-rodlike shape of ∼50 nm size (Figure 1e). The high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image of one representative NP displays a d-spacing of 0.279 nm, matching
with the (110) plane of monoclinic CuO (Figure 1f). Furthermore, the corresponding fast Fourier transform (FFT) and XRD patterns consistently manifest the monoclinic CuO crystalline structure with (002), (111), and (100) as the characteristic diffraction planes (Figure 1d,g). Next, we investigated the effect the PVDF coating exerts on the activity and selectivity of CO2RR on the CuO electrode. To that end, constant potential electrolysis was performed for 15 min at potentials between −1.37 and −1.02 V vs the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) in CO2-saturated aqueous 0.5 M KHCO3. The control experiment using a pristine CuO electrode gives H2 and C2H4 as major products along with minor amounts of CO, CH4, HCOOH, CH3COOH, C2H5OH, and n-C3H7OH in the entire examined potential range (Figures 2a and S3a). Notably, the faradaic efficiency of H2 (FEH2) first decreases from 51.7 to 31.4% by applying more negative potentials and starts to increase when the potential reaches −1.37 V vs RHE, while FEC2H4 keeps increasing to reach a plateau (∼28.5%) at −1.22 V vs RHE and tends to decrease at more negative potentials. In comparison, the CuO−PVDF electrode displays signifi-
cantly larger FEC2H4 at a given potential value, although the selectivity trend is not altered for the individual products (Figures 2b, S3b, and S4a). For example, at −1.12 V vs RHE, FEC2H4 is up to 32.0% for CuO−PVDF as opposed to the 16.7% obtained for CuO. At the same time, the hydrogen evolution reaction is greatly suppressed after PVDF mod-
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.0c03766 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 958−966
959
ification, in that the FEH2 decreases from 45.0% for CuO to 28.3% for CuO−PVDF. In the optimized case, the CuO− PVDF electrode can achieve FEC2H4 = 40.6% at −1.22 V vs RHE, which is among the highest in reported works under
similar electrolysis conditions (Table 1). It should be noted that the total faradaic efficiencies are below 100% on both CuO and CuO−PVDF electrodes. This is due to the fact that a part of the charge goes to the reduction of CuO to Cu, as the electrolysis potential is more negative than the reduction potential of CuO. Plots of the current density (|j|) against electrolysis potential provide further evidence of the beneficial impact from the PVDF modification (Figures 2c,d, S3c,d, S4b,c, and S5). First, the CuO−PVDF and CuO electrodes show comparable total current density (|j|total), independent of electrolysis potentials, e.g., |j|total = 11.7 mA cm
−2 for CuO−PVDF and 10.0 mA cm−2 for CuO at −1.12 V vs RHE (Figures 2c,d and S4b). Having said this, the partial current densities of the individual products show substantial variations. For example, while the CuO electrode exhibits |j|C2H4 = 1.4 mA cm
−2 at −1.12 V vs RHE, the CuO−PVDF shows |j|C2H4 = 3.8 mA cm −2, nearly three times larger. More so, the improved |j|C2H4 of CuO−PVDF, as compared to CuO, is a general observation across the entire potential range examined (Figure S4c). At the same time, the CuO−PVDF electrode shows a smaller |j|H2 than that of CuO, regardless of the electrolysis potential. For the other products formed, there are no obvious differences in the partial current densities of the two electrode types. On this basis, we may conclude that the presence of the porous PVDF layer on CuO significantly enhances the electrocatalytic activity of CuO-derived electrodes toward C2H4 production in CO2RR. A profound feature of the porous PVDF polymer is that it, by and large, causes no significant change to the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA), which decreases slightly from 0.129 to 0.116 cm2 after PVDF modification as determined from chronoamperometric experiments on the redox probe K3Fe(CN)6 in 0.1 M KCl (Figure S6). This is a notable improvement compared with the octadecanethiol modification protocol previously reported where a dense coverage led to a significant decrease of ECSA from 21 to 3 × 10−3 cm2 cm−2 (the unit cm2 cm−2 indicates the ECSA of the dendritic electrode versus that of a flat Cu electrode) and, as a result, activity loss.31
The durability of modified electrodes is an important issue to address, which in our study was done by performing prolonged electrolysis at −1.12 V vs RHE over 6 h (Figure 2e,f). Here, we find that the CuO electrode shows a gradual decay in both FEC2H4 (from 17.7 to 8.8%) and |j|C2H4 (from 2.0 to 1.3 mA cm−2). In comparison, both FEC2H4 and |j|C2H4 of CuO−PVDF remain almost constant over the same electrolysis period, fluctuating around 30% and 3.5 mA cm−2, respectively. Thus, the introduction of the PVDF coating is highly beneficial for the long-term performance of the electrode. One likely reason for the deactivation of the CuO electrode is poisoning of the active sites by trace-level metal impurities (i.e., Fe2+ and Zn2+) from the electrolyte.5,46 In fact, the stability of the CuO electrode could be markedly enhanced after purifying the electrolyte using a pre-electrolysis process (Figure S8). The high stability of the CuO−PVDF electrode can be attributed to the ability of the stably coated PVDF layer (as indicated by SEM and XPS; Figures S9 and S10) to limit the diffusion of water to the electrode surface. This prevents impurities in the aqueous electrolyte from reaching the Cu active site during long-term electrolysis.47
The morphology, crystallinity, and oxidation state of Cu are known to be the most essential features determining the CO2RR activity.
37,48 To figure out the effect that the PVDF modification exerts on these features, we compared the properties of the CuO NPs in the CuO and CuO−PVDF electrodes before and after CO2RR using SEM, TEM, XRD, and XPS. It should be noted that the PVDF layer was removed in the case of CuO−PVDF by washing with N,Ndimethylformamide (DMF) to offer a better view of the NPs. The SEM images reveal no obvious difference between CuO and CuO−PVDF even after 6 h electrolysis (Figure S11). In addition, TEM images show that the CuO NPs tend to fragment into small-sized domains during CO2RR, regardless of the presence of PVDF (Figures S12 and S13). In other words, PVDF seems to have no influence on the morphology change of CuO-derived catalysts. XRD was used to study the evolution of the crystalline structures of the CuO NPs for both electrodes (Figure S14). Initially, a typical XRD pattern of the monoclinic CuO crystalline structure (JCPDS #45-0937) is seen. After 15 min electrolysis, the XRD patterns point to a cubic Cu crystalline structure (JCPDS #04-0836) with (111) as the main diffraction peak and (100) as the accompanied peak for both electrodes. This demonstrates that the crystallinity change of Cu is not affected by the PVDF coating during CO2RR, with the only difference being that a small fraction of CuO for the CuO−PVDF electrode is left unreduced due to close contact with PVDF. Previously, density functional theory (DFT) calculations have shown that Cu(111) favors the C2H4 production over CH4 at high local surface pH values and relatively negative potentials, in line with our experimental results.49−51
XPS was used to determine the oxidation state of Cu (Figure 3). The pristine CuO and CuO−PVDF electrodes both show a
peak at 933.7 eV in the 2p3/2 spectra, originating from Cu 2+. After 15 min electrolysis, the peak shifts to 932.5 eV, which may be ascribed to Cu+ or Cu0. To distinguish between Cu+ and Cu0, the Cu Auger LMM kinetic energy spectra were recorded and the modified Auger parameter α′ was determined by the formula α′ = BE(Cu 2p3/2) + KE(CuLMM), where BE(Cu 2p3/2) is the binding energy corresponding to the Cu 2p3/2 core levels and KE(CuLMM) is the kinetic energy of CuLMM. In the Cu Auger LMM region, a peak appears at 918.0 eV for both pristine CuO and CuO−PVDF, while it decreases to 917.0 eV after CO2RR, corresponding to Cu
+. Moreover, α′ was found to be 1851.7 eV for both pristine CuO and CuO− PVDF, while it decreased to 1849.5 eV after 15 min electrolysis. The latter value matches the characteristic parameter for Cu+. These results together corroborate the formation of Cu+ species.36 The prolonged electrolysis for 6 h does not alter the Cu species further. It should be noted that the washing with DMF does not exert influence on the XPS spectra, as the CuO electrode with no exposure to DMF shows the same XPS spectra as CuO−PVDF after CO2RR. The inconsistency in the nature of the Cu species determined by XPS (Cu+) and XRD (Cu0) may very well originate in XPS being a surface technique, with an analysis depth of <10 nm, while XRD analyzes the entire bulk material.52 It seems plausible that the surface atoms of Cu0 formed under CO2RR conditions could be reoxidized during the XPS ex situ measurements, thus giving rise to the Cu+ signal. Cyclic voltammetry substantiates that Cu2+ is converted to Cu0 at −1.12 V vs RHE for both electrodes (Figure S15), as a broad and irreversible reductive wave is observed between 0.2 and −0.6 V vs RHE on the first cycle.53 This broad peak is also observable in an argon-saturated electrolyte, indicating that it originates from reduction of CuO and cannot be associated with reactions originating from the presence of CO2 (Figure S16). Furthermore, Cu0 is not oxidized back to Cu2+ or Cu+, as no oxidation wave is observed on the backward sweep and, in addition, the reduction wave disappears on the second and third voltammetric cycles (Figure S15). With the complete reduction of CuO to metallic Cu, this suggests that Cu0 is the
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.0c03766 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 958−966
961
species responsible for the electroreduction of CO2 on both CuO and CuO−PVDF. Altogether, these results suggest that the improvement in the
CO2RR performance provided by the presence of the PVDF coating does not originate from induced changes in the oxidation state, crystallinity, or morphology of the Cu species. Instead, PVDF must play a much more direct role. Previously, polymers with amine and other basic nitrogen moieties, i.e., poly(acrylamide) and poly(4-vinylpyridine), have been suggested to promote CO2RR by stabilizing intermediates such as *CO or the *CO−CO dimer through hydrogen-bonding or Lewis acid−base interactions.5,27 For the PVDF polymer with fluorine atoms attached to the carbon chains (Figure S17), such interactions should be negligible. It is also important to emphasize that the formed hydrocarbon products do not originate from PVDF itself as no products but H2 was formed if the electrode was fabricated from depositing PVDF alone on the carbon paper (Figure S18). What is then left as one of the potential factors being responsible for the boosting of the CO2to-C2H4 conversion is the change in interfacial hydrophilicity/ hydrophobicity induced by PVDF and its direct effect on the transport of the water serving as a proton source in CO2RR. To verify this hypothesis, another hydrophobic polymer, PE,
and two hydrophilic polymers, PVA having a protic functionality and PVP with an aprotic functionality (Figure S17), were utilized to modify the CuO electrode. Once again, the loading of each polymer was 0.25 mg cm−2 on carbon paper (see Experimental Section). In the cases of PVA and PVP, a small amount of Nafion (0.023 mg cm−2) was added as a binder to avoid the dissolution of the polymers. The effect from Nafion on the CO2RR activity and selectivity is expected to be small as deduced from water contact angle (WCA) measurements, where the CuO, CuO−PVA, and CuO−PVP electrode surfaces with a WCA in the range of 67−85° all are found to be hydrophilic, regardless of the presence of Nafion (Figure 4a and Table S1). In comparison, the WCAs of the electrodes are located in the hydrophobic region of 127.3 and 126.4° after modification with PE and PVDF, respectively.
Electrolysis experiments reveal that the impact of the two hydrophilic polymers (PVA and PVP) is negligible on the C2H4 selectivity, while FEH2 increases slightly when compared with pristine CuO (Figure 4b). In contrast, the hydrophobic PE gives rise to a dramatic increase in FEC2H4, accompanied by a decline in FEH2. This trend for CuO−PE along with the concomitant increase in |j|C2H4 is very similar to what is seen for CuO−PVDF. The conclusion is thus that hydrophobic polymers can greatly enhance CO2 reduction to C2H4, whereas hydrophilic polymers mainly facilitate the hydrogen evolution process. Furthermore, a plot of FEC2H4 against WCA shows that larger WCAs result in higher FEC2H4, suggesting that the effect of polymer modifiers is structure-nonspecific and related to the hydrophobicity (see CuO−PVDF and CuO−PE in Figure S19). At least, this is so on the larger picture, although other effects such as proton shuttling may come into play if functional groups (i.e., hydroxyl in PVA and amide in PVP) are present in the polymer, especially when the difference in WCA is small.54
To uncover the importance of interfacial hydrophobicity on CO2 reduction, we conducted molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the mass transport behavior in the aqueous solution using Gromacs (version 2019.1).55,56 A water box was first built with a cell size of 3.45 nm × 3.45 nm × 3.45 nm (Figure S20a). Ten PVDF oligomers (20 monomer units) were put into the box to investigate the influence of PVDF on the water diffusion (Figure S20b and Table S2). The diffusion coefficient was calculated according to the mean square displacement during 1 ns in an NVT (i.e., constant number of molecules, volume, and temperature) MD simulation at 298 K (Figure S21). Notably, while the diffusion coefficient of bulk water is 2.35 × 10−9 m2 s−1, it decreases to 1.81 × 10−9 m2 s−1 in the presence of PVDF (Table S4). Thus, the hydrophobic PVDF layer greatly limits the diffusion of water to the electrode surface, resulting in the suppression of hydrogen evolution and, as a consequence, enhancement of CO2RR. The dependency of the CO2RR activity on water diffusion becomes further evident using D2O as a solvent, considering that the self-diffusion coefficient of D2O (1.87 × 10
−9 m2 s−1) is lower than that of H2O.
57 Although the total current density is not affected significantly for either of the CuO and CuO− PVDF electrodes (Figures S5 and S22), the FEH2/D2 of CuO decreases significantly from 44.7 to 16.4% upon replacing H2O with D2O. Meanwhile, the selectivity of C2H4/C2D4 increases from 16.7 to 29.1% (Figure 4c). A similar trend is seen for CuO−PVDF when going to D2O, although the changes are not as significant as with CuO. Limited water diffusion can further change the concentration profiles of the species (CO2, HCO3 −, CO3
2−, and OH−) in the 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte. 58,59 Among these species, the OH− close to the electrode surface, generated in the CO2/H2O reduction, plays a particularly important role in the CO2RR activity.20 The concentration profiles of these species can be constructed by solving a series of partial differential mass transport equations based on the calculated diffusion coefficients (Figures 4d and S23 with a detailed discussion in Section 1.2 in the Supporting Information).60 The boundary layer is assumed to be 50 μm in all cases. Figure 4d shows that the increase in OH− concentration going from the bulk solution to the surface is larger for the CuO−PVDF electrode than the CuO electrode, especially in
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.0c03766 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 958−966
962
the PVDF layer. While the surface pH is calculated to be 9.2 at the CuO electrode, it increases to 9.4 with the PVDF coating present due to the restricted diffusion of water therein. Meanwhile, the CO2 concentration at the CuO−PVDF electrode surface maintains a relatively high value of 28.2 mM (Figure S23a), which is only slightly lower than that in the bulk solution (34.2 mM), ensuring good CO2 accessibility to the electrode. In this case, the consequence of having a higher local pH on the electrode surface as for CuO−PVDF is that it suppresses better the hydrogen evolution reaction to favor the CO2-to-C2H4 conversion. This result is consistent with previous DFT calculations as well as experimental results showing that high local pH favors the *CO−CO dimerization pathway, thus facilitating the further conversion of CO to form

sections.heading: C2H4.
sections.text: 51,61 At the same time, the high local pH kinetically inhibits the C1 pathways going through *COH and *CHO intermediates, which would produce CH4. Finally, we consider the cost effectiveness of our electrode modification procedure using organic molecules/polymers. Most previous reports have used a wet-chemical procedure to modify the electrodes, which requires the employment of either specialized technique under an inert atmosphere,62 or high temperatures,63 or long reaction times.64 In our system, we used a simple physical drop-coating method to modify the electrode with a polymer layer (e.g., PVDF and PE). Furthermore, this kind of physical coating approach could be readily scaled up, implying that the used physical coating method for electrode modification would be highly costeffective.

sections.heading: 3. CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: We have elucidated the role of Cu−electrolyte interfaces in CO2 reduction in aqueous solutions by modifying CuO electrodes with a series of polymers, including PVDF, PE, PVA, and PVP. For PVDF-modified electrodes, the faradaic efficiency (32.0%) of C2H4 production doubles, the partial current density (3.8 mA cm−2) almost triples, and the stability improves, as compared to the bare CuO electrode. A similar performance improvement is observed with a similarly hydrophobic PE coating, while modification with the hydrophilic PVA and PVP polymers brings no improvement whatsoever. The governing factor for this favorable effect of the inert PVDF and PE polymers is the hydrophobic environment they create on the Cu surface. It cannot be attributed to the specific adoption of polymer structures or changes in the oxidation state, crystallinity, and morphology of the Cu species triggered by the polymer modification. Instead, modeling of the interface suggests that in hydrophobic polymer coatings with more restricted water diffusion, the hydrogen evolution becomes suppressed because of a higher surface pH, thus favoring the reduction of CO2 to C2H4. We expect that our findings may serve as a guide for the future design of Cubased catalysts by highlighting the importance of interfacial manipulation for Cu-catalyzed CO2 reductions. An important issue to consider in future studies is the extent to which the CO2/H2O/electrolyte transport behavior and thus the product selectivity can be modulated by altering the thickness, porosity, and hydrophobicity of the PVDF layer.

sections.heading: 4. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
4.1. Chemicals. All chemicals were obtained from commercial suppliers and used without further purification.
CuO NPs (<50 nm), poly(vinylidene difluoride) (PVDF,Mw = 534 000), polyethylene (PE, Mw = 35 000), poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP, Mw = 10 000), and poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA, Mw = 67 000) were supplied by Sigma-Aldrich. HPLC-grade solvents were used in all experiments. N,NDimethylformamide (DMF) and methanol were purchased from VWR Chemicals, while dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, ≥99.9%), cyclohexane, and 2-propanol were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich.
4.2. Preparation of Working Electrodes. Carbon papers (FuelCellStore, Toray 060) were used as working electrodes after cleaning with water and acetone by sonication. CuO NPs were dispersed in DMF (5 mg mL−1) by sonication for 15 min. A volume of 50 μL of the resulting dispersion was drop-casted on each side (1 × 1 cm2) of a carbon paper and thoroughly dried in a fume hood. The resulting CuO-coated working electrode had a CuO loading of 0.25 mg cm−2. CuO−PVDF working electrodes were prepared by drop casting 50 μL of PVDF/DMF (5 mg mL−1) solution onto the previously prepared CuO electrodes (polymer loading = 0.25 mg cm−2). Other CuO−polymer working electrodes were prepared in the same way as CuO−PVDF, except that different solvents were used to dissolve the individual polymers [cyclohexane for PE, 2-propanol for PVP, and water/methanol (v/v = 2:3) for PVA]. In the cases of PVP and PVA, an additional 50 μL of Nafion solution (10 μL of commercial Nafion solution in 1 mL of 2-propanol) was drop-casted onto each side of the working electrode to avoid leaching of the two polymers during electrolysis. The neat Nafion loading was 0.023 mg cm−2, accounting for ∼10% of the loading of CuO and the polymer.
4.3. Characterization. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was performed on a Kratos Axis Ultra-DLD instrument operated with a monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source at a power of 150 W. The pressure in the main chamber during the analysis was kept around 10−11 bar. High-resolution spectra of Cu 2p and Cu LMM were recorded with a 20 eV pass energy and from the accumulation of four sweeps. CasaXPS software was used for fitting and C 1s at 285.0 eV for binding energy calibration. Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were performed with a Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diffractometer using monochromatic Cu Kα1 radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å). The data were collected in the 2θ window of 30− 80°. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were acquired on an FEI Nova NanoSEM 600 microscope at an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed on an FEI Talos F200X analytical STEM with an XFEG at 200 kV. To have better imaging of CuO NPs in the CuO−PVDF electrodes, the PVDF layer was removed by washing the CuO−PVDF electrode with 10 mL of DMF three times before characterization. The water contact angle was measured by the sessile drop method using an FTA1000 contact angle system (First Ten Angstroms, Inc.) at room temperature. The volume of the water droplets was 2.0 μL.
4.4. Cyclic Voltammetry. Cyclic voltammetric experiments were carried out using a CHI601D potentiostat connected to a three-electrode setup. The working electrode was a carbon paper coated with the CuO or polymer-modified CuO electrocatalyst using a platinum mesh as a counter electrode along with a leak-free Ag/AgCl reference electrode (ElectroCell LF-1). The potential measured against Ag/AgCl was converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acscatal.0c03766 ACS Catal. 2021, 11, 958−966
963
using the formula E (vs RHE) = E (vs Ag/AgCl) + 0.21 V + RT/F × ln10 × pH = E (vs Ag/AgCl) + 0.63 V. The supporting electrolyte was 0.5 M KHCO3 of pH 7.3 when saturated with CO2. 4.5. ECSA Measurement. The values of ECSA were
determined by chronoamperometry using K3Fe(CN)6 as a redox probe (Figure S6b). The chronoamperometric response was recorded for 1 s (with an interval of 0.001 s) after stepping the potential from 1.0 V to 0.5 V vs RHE in argon-purged 0.1 M KCl. The applied potential of 0.5 V vs RHE was set to be ∼300 mV more negative than the peak potential (∼0.80 V vs RHE; Figure S6a) to ensure that the reduction of K3Fe(CN)6 would be in the diffusion-limited regime. The ECSA values were calculated from the Cottrell equation65
π =i nFAC D t
In this expression, i is the current, n = 1, D = 4.34 × 10−6 cm2 s−1, F is the Faraday constant (96485 C mol−1), A is the electrochemically active surface area, and C is the concentration of K3Fe(CN)6 (5 × 10
−6 mol cm−3). By plotting i versus t−1/2 and extracting the slope from the linear part, ECSA can be determined (Figure S6c). 4.6. Controlled Potential Electrolysis and Gaseous
Product Analysis. The electrochemical CO2 reduction experiments were conducted in a home-made two-compartment H cell with the two chambers separated by a glass frit. The supporting electrolyte was 0.5 M KHCO3 of pH 7.3 when saturated with CO2. The three-electrode system consisting of a platinum mesh as the counter electrode, Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode, and CuO(-polymer) catalysts supported on a carbon paper as the working electrode was connected to the CHI601D potentiostat. Short-term electrolysis of CO2 was performed at a fixed potential for 15 min. Gaseous products (H2, CO, CH4, and C2H4) were quantified by an Agilent Technologies 7890B gas chromatography system equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and flame ionization detector (FID). The gas mixture was separated on an Agilent Select Permanent Gases/CO2 capillary column set consisting of two parallel columns that combined CP-Molsieve 5 Å for permanent gas analysis and CP-PoraBONDQ for CO2 analysis. The detector temperature was held at 200 °C and the oven at 45 °C. Ar was used as the carrier gas flowing at 14 mL min−1. The injection was performed with a 250 μL gas-tight syringe from SGE Analytical Science. Quantification of gas products was performed from calibration curves obtained by injecting known volumes of the pure gas mixed in CO2. 4.7. Identification and Quantification of Products in
an Electrolyte. After each bulk electrolysis at a constant potential, 700 μL of catholyte was syringed out from the electrochemical cell and mixed with 35 μL of internal standard containing 10 mM DMSO.66 This mixture was transferred to a nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) sample tube and analyzed by 1H NMR spectroscopy using a 400 MHz spectrometer (Bruker 400 spectrometer) to identify the products in the electrolyte. The signal of water was suppressed using a presaturation sequence. The 1H peak area of each product was compared to the 1H peak area of DMSO to quantify concentrations.
